findings.title: Multiple crypto providers no longer fail fast; ties in order() are resolved arbitrarily
findings.body: Before this change, detectProvider threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath. Now it silently sorts by order() descending and takes the first. All built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) use order 200, so a misconfigured classpath containing, for example, both keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402 — previously a clear startup error — now results in an arbitrary winner (stable sort keeps ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order, which varies by environment), with the losing provider only mentioned in a debug log. Consider restoring fail-fast behavior when the highest order is shared by more than one discovered provider.

findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider gains a new abstract method order(). Any existing third-party or custom CryptoProvider implementation compiled against the previous version of this interface will now fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError, because detectProvider invokes order() on every discovered provider during sorting (even when only one provider is present), and implementations fail to compile against the new interface. Declaring it as a default method (e.g. 'default int order() { return 100; }') would preserve backward compatibility while still allowing ordering.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK keystore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as '@return BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider', but this implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. whatever JDK provider implements the default keystore type (typically SUN/SunJSSE), never BouncyCastle. Consequently CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() (and hence BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) yields a non-BouncyCastle provider; any consumer that passes it to a JCA getInstance(..., provider) call for BC-only algorithms will fail, with no error pointing at the real cause. If this module intentionally ships without BouncyCastle, returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or explicitly documenting the deviation would be less misleading.

findings.title: Dead leftover encoder writes in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write rBigInteger and sBigInteger into them, and then discard the results; the actual return statement immediately below builds brand-new encoders. This has no functional effect but performs pointless allocation and DER encoding on every signature conversion and looks like leftover scaffolding from development. The two statements should be deleted.

findings.title: Round-trip test only proves the two converters are consistent inverses of each other
findings.body: The test asserts only that asn1derToConcatenatedRS followed by concatenatedRSToASN1DER followed by asn1derToConcatenatedRS returns the same bytes (rsConcat equals rsConcat2). Both methods could be wrong in complementary ways and the test would still pass — in the extreme, if both were identity functions the assertion holds while every ES256/384/512 signature produced or verified through them would be invalid. The test should validate against an independent reference: e.g. check rsConcat has the expected raw length and content relative to the JDK-produced DER signature, verify the re-encoded DER with java.security.Signature.verify(), or use a known test vector.

findings.title: Creating an AuthzClient now installs the minimal provider as JVM-global CryptoIntegration state
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(...), which sets the static JVM-global cryptoProvider if it is not already set. In an application that embeds the authz client and later calls CryptoIntegration.init(...) itself (expecting to install a fully functional provider), that later init is silently a no-op, and every CryptoIntegration.getProvider() caller in the JVM receives AuthzClientCryptoProvider, which throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.") for nearly all methods (getSignature, getPemUtils, getKeyPairGen, getX509CertFactory, ...). If this global side effect is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise consider initializing lazily only when crypto is actually needed or scoping the provider to the client.
